steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper on how well large language models understand graphs, comparing text, motif and image ways of encoding graph structure in prompts for node classification. Include the motivation, our contributions and the key findings.

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Large Language Models (LLMs) are being used more and more in areas that have graph structures built in, like social network analysis, drug discovery and recommendation systems. But they have limitations, because they rely on unstructured text and it is hard to incorporate new data into them after training. Graph-structured data can help with these issues, since it gives a nuanced and flexible representation of relationships in the real world.

There has been progress on interpreting multi-modal information, but integrating graph understanding into LLMs is still a developing area. One current challenge is that LLMs have difficulty processing complex graph-structured data directly, so innovative input encoding and prompt design are needed for the different graph tasks. Current research usually uses limited setups, with small real-world graphs or synthetic graphs. This shows a gap in how to effectively incorporate large real-world graphs into LLMs, because of their context window constraints. So text-only encoding may not be the best approach for large and complex graph structures.

In this paper we investigate how different modalities affect the encoding of global and local graph structures. We focus on node classification tasks and compare three modalities: Text, Motif and Image (See Figure 1). The text modality gives detailed local insights, but it gets verbose for large graphs and often goes over the input limits of models like GPT-4. We suggest the Motif modality to address this, since it captures the essential patterns around a node and gives a balanced local-global perspective. We also propose the Image modality, which uses fewer tokens to show a more global view of the node's neighborhood, and this is helped by the vision capabilities of the newly released GPT-4V. Finding the best prompt input format is a complex challenge, and the text modality encoding needs a lot more exploration than the image modality, which is simpler and more human-readable. In our evaluations we use a combination of metrics to balance informativeness and how concise the prompt is, for all the modalities.

- Contributions
  - breadth-first analysis: text, image, motif in graph-structure prompting; LLMs + vision-language models; node classification
  - depth-first analysis: factors affecting each modality
  - GraphTMI benchmark: hierarchy of graphs, prompts, encoding modalities

- Findings + outlook
  - 1) image beats text when balancing token limits vs crucial info
  - 2) choice depends on task difficulty (homophily, motif counts): image for medium, motif for harder
  - 3) edge encoding function, graph structure, graph sampling affect text modality
  - 4) motif attachment info matters more than motif count
  - 5) image readability (human) correlates with better performance
  - LLMs still behind Graph Neural Networks on real-world graphs; limits + potential of image understanding

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Large Language Models (LLMs) are being used more and more in areas that have graph structures built in, like social network analysis, drug discovery and recommendation systems. But they have limitations, because they rely on unstructured text and it is hard to incorporate new data into them after training. Graph-structured data can help with these issues, since it gives a nuanced and flexible representation of relationships in the real world.

There has been progress on interpreting multi-modal information, but integrating graph understanding into LLMs is still a developing area. One current challenge is that LLMs have difficulty processing complex graph-structured data directly, so innovative input encoding and prompt design are needed for the different graph tasks. Current research usually uses limited setups, with small real-world graphs or synthetic graphs. This shows a gap in how to effectively incorporate large real-world graphs into LLMs, because of their context window constraints. So text-only encoding may not be the best approach for large and complex graph structures.

In this paper we investigate how different modalities affect the encoding of global and local graph structures. We focus on node classification tasks and compare three modalities: Text, Motif and Image (See Figure 1). The text modality gives detailed local insights, but it gets verbose for large graphs and often goes over the input limits of models like GPT-4. We suggest the Motif modality to address this, since it captures the essential patterns around a node and gives a balanced local-global perspective. We also propose the Image modality, which uses fewer tokens to show a more global view of the node's neighborhood, and this is helped by the vision capabilities of the newly released GPT-4V. Finding the best prompt input format is a complex challenge, and the text modality encoding needs a lot more exploration than the image modality, which is simpler and more human-readable. In our evaluations we use a combination of metrics to balance informativeness and how concise the prompt is, for all the modalities.

Our main contributions are:

- We do a breadth-first analysis of different modalities, such as text, image and motif, for prompting with graph structure, using large language and vision-language models for node classification tasks.

- We also do a depth-first analysis of how different factors affect the performance of each encoding modality.

- We introduce GraphTMI, a new graph benchmark with a hierarchy of graphs, associated prompts and encoding modalities, which is meant to help the community understand the effects of graph structure when using LLMs.

Some key findings: 1) When we have to stay within token limits and still keep the crucial information, the image modality works better than the text modality for graph-related tasks. 2) Which encoding modality to choose for graph task classification depends on how difficult the task is, measured by homophily and motif counts; the image modality is best for medium-difficulty tasks and the motif modality for harder ones. 3) Things like the edge encoding function, the graph structure and the graph sampling technique affect node classification performance with the text modality. 4) Motif attachment information has a bigger impact on node classification than motif count information. 5) Image representations that are more human-readable have a positive effect on node classification performance.

Our research shows that LLMs are making progress with graph data processing, but they are still behind Graph Neural Networks when it comes to real-world graphs. This shows both the current limits and the future potential of LLMs with image understanding for graph interpretation and reasoning tasks.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used in areas with inherent graph structures such as social network analysis [1], drug discovery [2], and recommendation systems [3], but they face limitations due to their reliance on unstructured text and the difficulty of incorporating new data after training [4,5,6]. Graph-structured data can address these issues by providing a nuanced and flexible representation of real-world relationships.

While there has been progress in interpreting multi-modal information [7], integrating graph understanding into LLMs remains a developing area. Current challenges include LLMs’ difficulty in directly processing complex graph-structured data, which calls for innovative input encoding and prompt design [8,9] for various graph tasks. Current research typically uses limited setups with small real-world graphs [10] or synthetic ones [11], exposing a gap in effectively incorporating large real-world graphs into LLMs given their context window constraints. This suggests that text-only encoding may not be the optimal approach for complex, large graph structures.

This paper investigates the impact of different modalities for encoding global and local graph structures, focusing on node classification tasks, and compares three modalities: Text, Motif, and Image (See Figure 1). The Text modality offers detailed local insights but becomes verbose for large graphs [12], often exceeding the input limits of models like GPT-4. The Motif modality is suggested to address this, capturing essential patterns in a node’s vicinity for a balanced local-global perspective. In addition, the Image modality is proposed, using fewer tokens to convey a more global view of the node’s neighborhood, an approach enhanced by the vision capabilities of the newly released GPT-4V [13]. Finding the optimal prompt input format is a complex challenge, with text modality encoding requiring far more exploration than the simpler, more human-readable image modality. In our evaluations, we balance informativeness and prompt conciseness across all modalities using a combination of metrics.

Our main contributions are as follows:

- We conduct a breadth-first analysis of various modalities, such as text, image, and motif, in graph-structure prompting, using large language and vision-language models for node classification tasks.

- We also perform a depth-first analysis of how different factors influence the performance of each encoding modality.

- We introduce GraphTMI, a novel graph benchmark featuring a hierarchy of graphs, associated prompts, and encoding modalities, designed to further the community’s understanding of graph structure effects when using LLMs.

Some key findings: 1) When balancing the token limit constraint against preserving crucial information, the image modality is more effective than the text modality for graph-related tasks. 2) The choice of encoding modality for graph task classification depends on the task’s difficulty, as assessed by homophily and motif counts, with the image modality being optimal for medium-difficulty tasks and the motif modality for harder ones. 3) Factors such as the edge encoding function, graph structure, and graph sampling technique affect node classification performance with the text modality. 4) Motif attachment information has a larger impact on node classification than motif count information. 5) Image representations that correlate with human readability positively impact node classification performance.

Our research shows that while LLMs are progressing in graph data processing, they still fall short of Graph Neural Networks in handling real-world graphs, highlighting both the current limitations and the future potential of LLMs with image understanding in graph interpretation and reasoning tasks.
